claim: Bacterial small RNAs (sRNAs) are key elements of regulatory networks that modulate gene expression.
source: Bacterial small RNAs (sRNAs) are key elements of regulatory networks that modulate gene expression.
evidence: This is a general statement about sRNAs that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: RydC is an sRNA of Salmonella sp. and Escherichia coli.
source: The sRNA RydC of Salmonella sp. and Escherichia coli is an example of this class of riboregulators.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: RydC bears a 'seed' region that recognises specific transcripts through base-pairing.
source: Like many other sRNAs, RydC bears a 'seed' region that recognises specific transcripts through base-pairing, and its activities are facilitated by the RNA chaperone Hfq.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RydC activities are facilitated by the RNA chaperone Hfq.
source: Like many other sRNAs, RydC bears a 'seed' region that recognises specific transcripts through base-pairing, and its activities are facilitated by the RNA chaperone Hfq.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure of RydC in complex with E. coli Hfq was determined at 3.48 Å resolution.
source: The crystal structure of RydC in complex with E. coli Hfq at a 3.48 Å resolution illuminates how the protein interacts with and presents the sRNA for target recognition.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by crystallographic data in the methods and results sections.

claim: The natively unstructured termini of Hfq mediate distributed interactions that consolidate the protein-RNA complex.
source: Consolidating the protein–RNA complex is a host of distributed interactions mediated by the natively unstructured termini of Hfq.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural observations in the results section.

claim: Bacterial sRNAs are typically 50 to 300 nucleotides in length.
source: Bacterial sRNAs are typically 50 to 300 nucleotides in length (Storz et al., 2011), and each control expression of a distinct set of target mRNAs, which they recognise with high specificity and apparent precision.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Each sRNA controls expression of a distinct set of target mRNAs with high specificity and precision.
source: Bacterial sRNAs are typically 50 to 300 nucleotides in length (Storz et al., 2011), and each control expression of a distinct set of target mRNAs, which they recognise with high specificity and apparent precision.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Hfq is one of the major facilitators of sRNA activity in bacteria.
source: One of the major facilitators of sRNA activity in bacteria is the protein Hfq, which promotes pairing of an sRNA with its target mRNA in solution (Møller et al., 2002; Vogel and Luisi, 2011; Panja and Woodson, 2012; De Lay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Hfq promotes pairing of an sRNA with its target mRNA in solution.
source: One of the major facilitators of sRNA activity in bacteria is the protein Hfq, which promotes pairing of an sRNA with its target mRNA in solution (Møller et al., 2002; Vogel and Luisi, 2011; Panja and Woodson, 2012; De Lay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Hfq bears an α + β fold that is the signature of the highly conserved family of Sm/Lsm proteins.
source: Hfq bears an α + β fold that is the signature of the highly conserved family of Sm/Lsm proteins that draws members from all domains of life (Kambach et al., 1999; Wilusz and Wilusz, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations supporting the structural classification.

claim: Hfq of E. coli and other eubacteria forms a compact hexameric toroid.
source: Hfq of Escherichia coli and other eubacteria forms a compact hexameric toroid that presents two structurally non-equivalent concave surfaces for molecular recognition; these faces are referred to as the proximal and distal faces, with the former exposing an N-terminal α-helix (Schumacher et al., 2002; Link et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural description.

claim: The Hfq hexamer presents two structurally non-equivalent concave surfaces called the proximal and distal faces.
source: Hfq of Escherichia coli and other eubacteria forms a compact hexameric toroid that presents two structurally non-equivalent concave surfaces for molecular recognition; these faces are referred to as the proximal and distal faces, with the former exposing an N-terminal α-helix (Schumacher et al., 2002; Link et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural description.

claim: The proximal face of Hfq interacts preferentially with uridine-rich sequences.
source: According to these results, the proximal site interacts preferentially with uridine-rich sequences, while the distal site favours the binding of ARN or ARNN motifs (with R being a purine and N any nucleotide) (Schumacher et al., 2002; Link et al., 2009; Sauer and Weichenrieder, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the binding preference.

claim: The distal face of Hfq favours the binding of ARN or ARNN motifs.
source: According to these results, the proximal site interacts preferentially with uridine-rich sequences, while the distal site favours the binding of ARN or ARNN motifs (with R being a purine and N any nucleotide) (Schumacher et al., 2002; Link et al., 2009; Sauer and Weichenrieder, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the binding preference.

claim: The Hfq hexamer bears a convex circumferential rim that contributes to RNA binding.
source: In addition to the distal and proximal faces, the torus-shaped Hfq hexamer bears a convex circumferential rim that has recently been identified as a surface contributing to RNA binding (Sauer et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the identification of the rim as an RNA binding surface.

claim: RydC is involved in biofilm regulation.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that RydC is involved in biofilm regulation (Bordeau and Felden, 2014) as well as in the control of membrane stability through the positive regulation of an isoform of the cfa mRNA encoding cyclopropane fatty acid synthase (Fröhlich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: RydC controls membrane stability through positive regulation of an isoform of the cfa mRNA encoding cyclopropane fatty acid synthase.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that RydC is involved in biofilm regulation (Bordeau and Felden, 2014) as well as in the control of membrane stability through the positive regulation of an isoform of the cfa mRNA encoding cyclopropane fatty acid synthase (Fröhlich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: RydC is proposed to have a pseudoknot fold that exposes a 5′ seed sequence.
source: RydC is proposed to have a pseudoknot fold that exposes a 5′ seed sequence, and the in vivo stability of RydC requires Hfq (Antal et al., 2005; Fröhlich et al., 2013; Bordeau and Felden, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural prediction.

claim: The in vivo stability of RydC requires Hfq.
source: RydC is proposed to have a pseudoknot fold that exposes a 5′ seed sequence, and the in vivo stability of RydC requires Hfq (Antal et al., 2005; Fröhlich et al., 2013; Bordeau and Felden, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: The double mutant RydC-S1 (G37C and G39C) was predicted computationally to form a distinct structure with one short stem-loop at the 5′-end and a strong terminator hairpin at the 3′-end.
source: A double mutant of RydC (G37C and G39C within helix 1; hereafter, RydC-S1) was predicted computationally to form a distinct structure with one short stem-loop at the 5′-end and a strong terminator hairpin at the 3′-end (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Wild-type RydC is very stable in wild-type cells with a half-life greater than 32 minutes.
source: As previously shown (Fröhlich et al., 2013), RydC is very stable in wild-type cells (half-life (t1/2) >32 min), while RydC-S1 decayed rapidly (t1/2 ∼2 min).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: RydC-S1 decays rapidly with a half-life of approximately 2 minutes.
source: As previously shown (Fröhlich et al., 2013), RydC is very stable in wild-type cells (half-life (t1/2) >32 min), while RydC-S1 decayed rapidly (t1/2 ∼2 min).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The half-life of RydC is markedly reduced in hfq mutant cells to approximately 4 minutes.
source: In contrast, the half-life of RydC is already markedly reduced in hfq mutant cells (t1/2 ∼4 min) and there is some further acceleration of the decay rate for RydC-S1, matching that of RydC in the absence of Hfq.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: RydC stability depends on both the integrity of the pseudoknot fold and the ability to associate with the Hfq protein.
source: This observation led us to assume that RydC stability depends on both the integrity of the pseudoknot fold and the ability to associate with the Hfq protein.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental observations in Figure 1.

claim: Both wild-type RydC and RydC-S1 mutant bind Hfq in electrophoretic mobility shift assays.
source: Both the wild-type RydC and RydC-S1 mutant bind Hfq in electrophoretic mobility shift assays with in vitro synthesized RNA although the affinity of the mutant is lower than for the wild-type RydC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The affinity of RydC-S1 for Hfq is lower than that of wild-type RydC.
source: Both the wild-type RydC and RydC-S1 mutant bind Hfq in electrophoretic mobility shift assays with in vitro synthesized RNA although the affinity of the mutant is lower than for the wild-type RydC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The binding sites for RydC and RydC-S1 on Hfq overlap at least partially.
source: Competition experiments suggest that the binding sites for the RydC and RydC-S1 overlap at least partially (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from competition experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the crystal comprises one full Hfq hexamer and one RydC.
source: The asymmetric unit of the crystal comprises one full Hfq hexamer and one RydC (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The fold of RydC is consistent with the pseudoknot structure predicted from solution studies and sequence alignments.
source: The fold of the RydC is consistent with the pseudoknot structure predicted from solution studies and sequence alignments (Antal et al., 2005; Fröhlich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by the crystal structure.

claim: The RNA bridges two adjacent Hfq hexamers in the crystal lattice, effectively forming a distorted sandwich with a wedge-shape.
source: The RNA bridges two adjacent Hfq hexamers in the crystal lattice, effectively forming a distorted sandwich with a wedge-shape (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 3′-end of RydC interacts with the proximal face of the principle hexamer.
source: The 3′-end of the RNA interacts with the proximal face of the principle hexamer, while the 5′-end interacts with the upper portion of the lateral surface of another hexamer in the asymmetric unit (see below for details, paragraph 'Interactions of RydC with the lateral surface of Hfq').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The 5′-end of RydC interacts with the upper portion of the lateral surface of another hexamer in the asymmetric unit.
source: The 3′-end of the RNA interacts with the proximal face of the principle hexamer, while the 5′-end interacts with the upper portion of the lateral surface of another hexamer in the asymmetric unit (see below for details, paragraph 'Interactions of RydC with the lateral surface of Hfq').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Solution studies using analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) and multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALS) indicate that RydC can form a stable 1:1 complex with the Hfq hexamer under various buffer conditions when the components are present in unitary stoichiometry.
source: However, solution studies using analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) and multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALS) indicate that the RydC can form a stable 1:1 complex with the Hfq hexamer under various buffer conditions when the components are present in unitary stoichiometry (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: When Hfq is present at twice the concentration of RydC under low ionic strength conditions, some 2:1 Hfq:RydC species can be identified.
source: When Hfq is present at twice the concentration of RydC under low ionic strength conditions, some 2:1 Hfq:RydC species can be identified; moreover, a higher order complex can be observed by electrophoretic mobility shifts when Hfq is in excess over RNA (results not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by solution studies.

claim: The stoichiometry of Hfq/RNA complexes is very sensitive to solution conditions.
source: These observations suggest that the stoichiometry of Hfq/RNA complexes is very sensitive to solution conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the solution studies.

claim: The 1:1 complex is likely to represent the physiologically relevant species.
source: In vivo, it seems unlikely that one RydC can find two Hfq hexamers when the protein is limiting to total RNA (Wagner, 2013), and we suggest that the 1:1 complex is likely to represent the physiologically relevant species.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on in vivo considerations and cited literature.

claim: The 3′-end of RydC has a U-rich tail that facilitates Rho-independent transcription termination.
source: The 3′-end of RydC has a U-rich tail that - together with a strong hairpin structure - facilitates Rho-independent transcription termination and which is an important determinant for recognition of many sRNAs (Otaka et al., 2011; Sauer and Weichenrieder, 2011; Ishikawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the functional role of the U-rich tail.

claim: The U-rich tail of RydC is bound in a recessed channel on the proximal face of Hfq.
source: The RydC/Hfq structure reveals that the U-rich tail is bound in a recessed channel on the proximal face of Hfq.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Uridines U61, U62, and U64 (as well as C63) each forms an aromatic base stacking interaction with the ring of F42.
source: The electron density is not well defined in this region, and there may be disorder or multiple conformations of the polyU tail, but the features do show that uridines U61, U62, and U64 (as well as C63) each forms an aromatic base stacking interaction with the ring of F42 (Figure 3C; distances provided in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by structural data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: K56 forms hydrogen bonds with the O2 group of the uracils.
source: K56 forms hydrogen bonds with the O2 group of the uracils, consistent with the importance of this residue in binding RNA on the proximal face (Mikulecky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation supporting the importance of K56.

claim: There are likely hydrogen bonds between the uridine bases and Q41 and Q8.
source: The model indicates that there are likely to be hydrogen bonds between the uridine bases and Q41 and Q8, as well as between the furanose 2′ OH group with the imidazole group of H57.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural model.

claim: These interactions are consistent with the crystal structure of Salmonella Typhimurium Hfq/polyU.
source: These interactions are consistent with the crystal structure of Salmonella Typhimurium Hfq/polyU (Sauer and Weichenrieder, 2011; PDB code 2YLC) and with fluorescence quenching experiments for binding U6 (Robinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the consistency of the observed interactions.

claim: U24 stacks onto F39 and U23 packs onto U24.
source: On the exposed rim of the proximal face, U24 stacks onto F39 and U23 packs onto U24 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: U46 and U47 bases form similar interactions with the rim of Hfq in a neighbouring asymmetric unit.
source: The U46/U47 bases form similar interactions with the rim of Hfq in a neighbouring asymmetric unit (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: U24 and U47 contact N13 and likely make a hydrogen bonding interaction.
source: U24 and U47 contact N13 and likely make a hydrogen bonding interaction.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural model.

claim: Both U23/U24 and U46/U47 pairs are highly conserved in an alignment of the available RydC sequences.
source: Both U23/U24 and U46/U47 pairs are highly conserved in an alignment of the available RydC sequences (Fröhlich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the conservation.

claim: A chimeric RNA assembled from the RydC 5′-end (nt. 1 to 13) and the 3′-end of the sRNA MicA is as efficient in target gene regulation as the wild-type RydC.
source: Although highly conserved, the U23/U24 and U46/U47 pairs are not required for the base-pairing to the RydC target, cfa mRNA, because a chimeric RNA assembled from the RydC 5′-end (nt. 1 to 13) and the 3′-end of the sRNA MicA is as efficient in target gene regulation as the wild-type RydC (Fröhlich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Mutant RydC-LII had a reduced half-life (t1/2 ∼11 min) compared to wild-type RydC (t1/2 ∼32 min).
source: Compared to wild-type RydC (t1/2 ∼32 min), mutant RydC-LII had a reduced half-life (t1/2 ∼11 min).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Both variants RydC-LI and the double mutant RydC-LI/LII were less stable (t1/2 ∼2 min).
source: Both variants RydC-LI and the double mutant RydC-LI/LII were even less stable (t1/2 ∼2 min) and especially the RydC-LI and RydC-LI/LII variants were less potent than the wild-type to regulate the reporter target Cfa–GFP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: RydC-LI and RydC-LI/LII variants were less potent than the wild-type to regulate the reporter target Cfa–GFP.
source: Both variants RydC-LI and the double mutant RydC-LI/LII were even less stable (t1/2 ∼2 min) and especially the RydC-LI and RydC-LI/LII variants were less potent than the wild-type to regulate the reporter target Cfa–GFP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: The in vivo data suggest a requirement of the conserved U pairs in the loops of the RydC pseudoknot structure for RNA stability.
source: Thus, while functional conclusions may be limited at this point, our in vivo data suggest a requirement of the conserved U pairs in the loops of the RydC pseudoknot structure for RNA stability and indicate a functional importance for the interactions observed in the crystal structure of the complex.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the in vivo data in Figure 5.

claim: The observed U23/U24 and U46/U47 interactions with the rim region may account for the findings that E. coli Hfq has greater affinity for 16-mer polyU compared to the 6-mer U6.
source: The observed U23/U24 and U46/U47 interactions with the rim region may account for the findings from solution studies that E. coli Hfq has greater affinity for 16-mer polyU compared to the 6-mer U6, because the longer polymer could form the contacts in the recessed core with the U-rich 3′-end and simultaneously interact with the rim through F39 and N13.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observations and solution studies.

claim: Residues R16, R17, R19, and K47 form a lateral RNA binding surface in Salmonella Hfq.
source: Earlier studies identified residues R16, R17, R19, and K47 as forming a lateral RNA binding surface in Salmonella Hfq (Sauer et al., 2012; highlighted in cyan in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: R16 and R17 make phosphate backbone contacts near U23 and U24.
source: In our structure, R16 and R17 make phosphate backbone contacts near U23 and U24 (Figure 4A), while R19 and K47 are not interacting with the RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: R19 and K47 are not interacting with the RNA in the crystal structure.
source: In our structure, R16 and R17 make phosphate backbone contacts near U23 and U24 (Figure 4A), while R19 and K47 are not interacting with the RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Residues R16 and R17 belonging to Hfq in the neighbouring crystal unit cell are involved in the binding of the 5′-end of RydC.
source: Residues R16 and R17 belonging to Hfq in the neighbouring crystal unit cell are also involved in the binding of the 5′-end of RydC (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutations on the rim region do not impact on the ability of Hfq to bind sRNA sequences but rather on its capacity to stimulate annealing of sRNA with an mRNA target.
source: This may account for observations from previous studies showing that mutations on this region of the rim do not impact on the ability of Hfq to bind sRNA sequences but rather on its capacity to stimulate annealing of sRNA with an mRNA target (Panja et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Both the wild-type protein (HfqWT) and the Hfq rim mutant (HfqRim) have similar affinities and association rate constants for the immobilised cfa.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, both the wild-type protein (HfqWT) and the Hfq rim mutant (HfqRim) have similar affinities and association rate constants for the immobilised cfa.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: The binding affinity of HfqWT for cfa decreases by a factor of roughly 5 in the presence of RydC.
source: In the presence of RydC, the association of Hfq with cfa changes. The binding affinity of HfqWT for cfa decreases by a factor of roughly 5, suggesting that the formation of the Hfq–sRNA complex affects the Hfq affinity for the mRNA fragment.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: The presence of RydC decreases by an order of magnitude the association rate constant of Hfq for cfa.
source: Moreover, the presence of RydC decreases by an order of magnitude the association rate constant of Hfq for cfa.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: In the presence of RydC, the HfqRim mutant no longer has detectable binding to cfa.
source: Strikingly, in the presence of RydC, the HfqRim mutant no longer has detectable binding to cfa.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: The rim interactions are crucial for forming a productive sRNA:Hfq:mRNA assembly.
source: This finding suggests that the RydC interacts differently with HfqWT and the HfqRim lateral surface mutant in a way that perturbs cfa binding. Thus, the rim interactions shown in Figure 6A,B,C are crucial for forming a productive sRNA:Hfq:mRNA assembly.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the binding data in Figure 6D.

claim: The C-terminal regions of Hfq, beyond residue 70, are generally disordered.
source: The C-terminal regions of Hfq, beyond residue 70, are generally disordered, but density could be observed for some of the protomers into which the model could be partially extended.
evidence: This is stated based on the crystal structure.

claim: The C-terminal tails appear to be making distributive contacts over the surface of RydC.
source: Although poorly ordered, the C-terminal tails appear to be making distributive contacts over the surface of RydC.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The half-life of RydC was greatly reduced in the absence of the C-terminal end (t1/2 ∼5 min) and was comparable with the half-life observed for an hfq null mutant (t1/2 ∼4 min).
source: We observed that the half-life of RydC was greatly reduced in the absence of the C-terminal end (t1/2 ∼5 min) and was comparable with the half-life observed for an hfq null mutant (t1/2 ∼4 min).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: The affinity of purified Hfq truncated at residue 66 (Hfq66) for binding cfa is similar to that of the wild-type protein.
source: In vitro binding experiments show that the affinity of purified Hfq truncated at residue 66 (Hfq66) for binding cfa is similar to that of the wild-type protein; however, the presence of RydC decreases substantially the binding of Hfq66 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of RydC decreases substantially the binding of Hfq66 to cfa.
source: In vitro binding experiments show that the affinity of purified Hfq truncated at residue 66 (Hfq66) for binding cfa is similar to that of the wild-type protein; however, the presence of RydC decreases substantially the binding of Hfq66 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C-terminal tails are important for facilitating the formation of the sRNA:mRNA:Hfq ternary complex.
source: These observations suggest that the C-terminal tails are important for facilitating the formation of the sRNA:mRNA:Hfq ternary complex.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: The C-terminal tails appear to influence the rate of Hfq–RNA complex formation.
source: The C-terminal tails appear to influence the rate of Hfq–RNA complex formation, as indicated by the order-of-magnitude lower on-rate of Hfq66 compared to HfqWT for binding cfa (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the binding data in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The crystal structure of RydC/Hfq suggests key elements of molecular recognition of this effector complex.
source: The crystal structure of RydC/Hfq suggests key elements of molecular recognition of this effector complex.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the structural findings.

claim: The consensus Hfq binding site on many sRNAs includes a U–U dinucleotide associated with an unpaired region.
source: Based on results from in vivo crosslinking and RNA sequencing from enterohemorrhagic E. coli, it has been proposed that the consensus Hfq binding site on many sRNAs includes a U–U dinucleotide associated with an unpaired region (Tree et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The unpaired region is required to engage the U–U step on the rim.
source: Our results are consistent with this prediction and provide a structural rationalisation: the unpaired region is required to engage the U–U step on the rim.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural data.

claim: Interactions with the rim may account for the capacity of longer U-tracts to bind Hfq more strongly.
source: Interactions with the rim may account for the capacity of longer U-tracts to bind Hfq more strongly (Murina et al., 2013; Panja et al., 2013), since these are anticipated to bridge between the rim and the 3′-polyU-binding pore.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural data with citations to support the binding observations.

claim: The rim might be the binding site for the internal U-rich region in SgrS that is required for stable association with Hfq.
source: The rim might also be the binding site for the internal U-rich region in SgrS that is required for stable association with Hfq (Ishikawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as speculation with a citation to support the requirement for the U-rich region.

claim: The 1:1 complex is the physiologically relevant species in vivo.
source: We propose that the 1:1 complex is the physiologically relevant species in vivo and that the sandwiching complex we observe in the crystal is likely to mimic a folding intermediate en route to forming a closed 1:1 RydC:Hfq complex.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on solution data and in vivo considerations.

claim: The sandwiching complex observed in the crystal is likely to mimic a folding intermediate en route to forming a closed 1:1 RydC:Hfq complex.
source: We propose that the 1:1 complex is the physiologically relevant species in vivo and that the sandwiching complex we observe in the crystal is likely to mimic a folding intermediate en route to forming a closed 1:1 RydC:Hfq complex.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the crystal structure and solution data.

claim: The C-termini of Vibrio cholerae and E. coli Hfq are natively unstructured.
source: Solution studies indicate that the C-termini of Vibrio cholerae and E. coli Hfq are natively unstructured (Beich-Frandsen et al., 2011; Vincent et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: A structural condensation of the C-terminal domains with sRNA binding is consistent with data from X-ray and neutron solution scattering.
source: A structural condensation of the C-terminal domains with sRNA binding is also consistent with data from X-ray and neutron solution scattering (Henderson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The distributive interactions of the C-terminal domain are not expected to provide specificity to the recognition but may enhance the stability of equilibrium complexes as well as boosting the association rates.
source: The distributive interactions of the C-terminal domain are not expected to provide specificity to the recognition but may enhance the stability of equilibrium complexes as well as boosting the association rates by increasing the effective molecular encounter radius.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural and binding data.

claim: Deletion of the C-terminal extension decreases binding to mRNAs.
source: The distributive interaction may account for the finding that deletion of the C-terminal extension decreases binding to mRNAs (Večerek et al., 2008) and that the C-terminal tail can bind to some RNA species (Robinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: M. jannaschii Hfq is generally able to complement a Salmonella hfq null mutant.
source: M. jannaschii Hfq is generally able to complement a Salmonella hfq null mutant; however, the distribution of associated sRNAs recovered from pull-down experiments varies greatly compared to the wild-type.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A second class of sRNAs is strongly affected by the absence of the C-terminal end, including RydC and several sRNAs highly abundant in the wild-type.
source: While a number of Salmonella sRNAs (including, for example, the Hfq-dependent SroC, InvR, and GcvB) are not reduced in their cellular abundance, a second class of sRNAs is strongly affected by the absence of the C-terminal end. This latter group includes RydC and also several sRNAs highly abundant in the wild-type (e.g., RprA, SdsR, and ArcZ), and it is tempting to speculate that this subpopulation of sRNAs is associated with Hfq through supporting interactions with the C-terminal tail.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the cited study.

claim: The differing roles of the tails for different sRNAs may account for the apparently conflicting results reported in the literature on the effects of the C-terminus on sRNA binding and activity.
source: The differing roles of the tails for different sRNAs may account for the apparently conflicting results reported in the literature on the effects of the C-terminus on sRNA binding and activity (Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as speculation with a citation.

claim: The C-terminal tails have different lengths in different Hfq homologs, and it is likely that their role differs in different species.
source: Finally, it should be noted that the C-terminal tails have different lengths in different Hfq homologs, and it is likely that their role differs in different species (Vincent et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the observation.

claim: The interactions of natively unstructured regions with RNA may be important in other nucleic acid/protein complexes.
source: As a general principle, the interactions of natively unstructured regions with RNA may be important in other nucleic acid/protein complexes (Tompa and Csermely, 2004; Kucera et al., 2011; Jonas and Izaurralde, 2013), and they can contribute to cooperative binding (Hunter and Anderson, 2009; Motlagh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the general principle.

claim: The model predicts that the 5′ seed will be exposed and available for interaction with the target to form a duplex region that binds to the convex rim of the Hfq hexamer.
source: Based on the current crystal structure, including the lattice interactions observed, and on other available structural and biophysical data, we propose a speculative model for the ternary complex of Hfq/sRNA and mRNA target (Figure 8). The model shares some similarity to the schematic proposed by Panja et al. (2013) and predicts that the 5′ seed will be exposed and available for interaction with the target to form a duplex region that binds to the convex rim of the Hfq hexamer.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative model based on the structural data and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Co-crystals of full length E. coli Hfq and Salmonella RydC were obtained that diffracted to 3.48 Å resolution.
source: Co-crystals of full length E. coli Hfq and Salmonella RydC were obtained that diffracted to 3.48 Å resolution, and the crystal structure of the RydC–Hfq complex was solved by molecular replacement using a model of the structured hexameric core of E. coli Hfq (i.e., lacking the C-terminal residues beyond amino acid 65).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the crystallographic work.

claim: The crystal structure of the RydC–Hfq complex was solved by molecular replacement using a model of the structured hexameric core of E. coli Hfq.
source: Co-crystals of full length E. coli Hfq and Salmonella RydC were obtained that diffracted to 3.48 Å resolution, and the crystal structure of the RydC–Hfq complex was solved by molecular replacement using a model of the structured hexameric core of E. coli Hfq (i.e., lacking the C-terminal residues beyond amino acid 65).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the structure determination.

claim: Unbiased, interpretable density for the RNA was apparent in the early maps calculated from the positioned protein hexamer.
source: Unbiased, interpretable density for the RNA was apparent in the early maps calculated from the positioned protein hexamer, and a model for most of RydC could be fitted into the electron density (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows a map in which the RNA was omitted from the refinement and phase calculations).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
